Objet : Recommandations de sécurisation des liaisons inter-sites, à destination des clients de ces offres.
Annexe : Liens et références
Depuis plusieurs années, l’Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information (ANSSI) a constaté de multiples compromissions de réseaux de télécommunications [1]. Dans certains cas, les attaquants ont pu profiter de l’absence de chiffrement sur certaines liaisons (fixes / mobiles / satellites) ainsi qu’au sein de ces réseaux, dits backbone, pour procéder à des opérations d’espionnage stratégique de communications.

Comme le rappellent l’ANSSI et l’Autorité de régulation des communications électroniques, des postes et de la distribution de la presse (ARCEP) dans le guide numérique des entreprises [2], les offres de réseaux privés proposées par les opérateurs de communications électroniques peuvent être utilisées pour porter des liaisons inter-sites. Les offres commercialisées par les opérateurs de communications électroniques n’incluent pas toujours par défaut les mécanismes permettant au client de s’assurer de la confidentialité et de l’intégrité des communications, y compris en cas d’accès au réseau opérateur par un attaquant. En effet, les technologies comme MPLS, les réseaux satellites, ou les réseaux mobiles privés de type «slice» ou «APN» ne chiffrent pas nativement les communications.

Les offres présentées comme des VPN MPLS ne chiffrent pas systématiquement les communications, à l’inverse des VPN TLS ou IPsec bien configurés.

Pour pallier à ces faiblesses, l’ANSSI recommande des actions de sécurisation minimales à mettre en œuvre. Ces recommandations s’adressent en premier lieu aux clients de ces solutions de réseaux privés en France. En cas de besoin, il est important de solliciter l’opérateur de communications électroniques ou l’intégrateur retenu, pour savoir quelles sont les mesures de sécurité supportées par la solution de connectivité fournie. Il convient de clarifier au moment du contrat les responsabilités de chaque partie en termes de maintien en conditions de sécurité, d’administration, de durcissement, de patch, etc.

Mesures de sécurité minimales à mettre en place

S’assurer du chiffrement des communications lorsqu’elles sortent du périmètre sous votre maîtrise, si possible de bout en bout pour interdire tout accès au trafic à partir du réseau de l’opérateur ;
Vérifier les comptes existants sur les équipements de bordure déployés dans vos réseaux pour remplacer, le cas échéant, l’ensemble des mots de passe et identifiants par défaut par des mots de passe complexes et robustes ;
Mettre en place un système de détection et de journalisation afin de vérifier que les équipements sous votre responsabilité n’ont pas été détournés pour effectuer des actions non autorisées sur l’infrastructure réseau ou les autres équipements clients ;
Appliquer les correctifs de sécurité dans les meilleurs délais sur les équipements sous votre responsabilité ;
En cas de besoin de disponibilité forte, assurer la redondance des accès réseau par des chemins physiquement séparés.

A noter pour le point 2 : dans certaines offres, l’équipement côté client est administré par l’opérateur. C’est donc son rôle de sécuriser l’administration de ces équipements, de les mettre à jour et de journaliser leurs activités. En tant que client, il reste possible de détecter si cet équipement est ou non utilisé comme point de pivot par un attaquant lorsque celui-ci attaque le réseau interne.

CVE-2026-136502 - SQL injection and redirected writes because the driver reads SQL text differently from the server
text:
8.1

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-136502
SQL injection and redirected writes because the driver reads SQL text differently from the server

psqlODBC scans statement text itself to substitute parameters, translate ODBC escapes, join batched statements and rewrite queries for updatable cursors. Where it read the text differently from the server, text the driver took for data ran as SQL, or a positioned write went to another table:

- An escape string constant written e'…' in lower case was not recognised as one, and '…' after a keyword ending in E, as in LIKE'…', was taken for one.
- A } inside a quoted literal ended an ODBC {d …}, {t …}, {ts …} or {escape …} sequence.
- Dollar-quote tags containing _ were not recognised, and an identifier starting with _ followed by $, such as _$$, was taken for the start of a dollar quote, so a parameter marker inside a literal was substituted.
- A trailing -- comment in one statement of a batched parameter array swallowed the next statement.
- Comments, literals longer than 255 bytes and escape strings were misread when the driver located the FROM and WHERE clauses of a query for an updatable cursor, and the text copied into the cursor's own queries could include SQL from inside a literal.
- A table name containing $ was cut at the $, and a quoted table name starting with , or ; ended the table list, so positioned updates, inserts and deletes went to another table.
- An integer parameter with an embedded NUL byte cut the query short.
- /*/ was taken for a comment that opens and closes, while the server reads it as one that only opens.
- ConnSettings was split at every semicolon, including one inside a quoted literal, so an application that puts an end user's value into a SET command there ran the rest of the value as SQL at connect time.

An end user who controls text the application puts into a statement, or a parameter value, can run SQL with the rights of the application's database role. A database user who can create a table with a crafted name can redirect another user's positioned writes to a table of their choosing.

Versions up to and including psqlODBC 18.00.0006 are affected.

title: CVE-2026-134070 - Improper input validation in the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3
text:
8.0

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-134070
Improper input validation in the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3

Improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions.

Because any user permitted to run the runbook selects which revision to run, this issue remains reachable in an affected Region until earlier revisions can no longer be run there. AWS is deprecating all revisions created before 2026-10-22 (UTC) in every Region and partition beginning January 15, 2027; until deprecation, earlier revisions remain runnable, so upgrading alone is not sufficient.

To remediate this issue:

1. Run the latest revision of the runbook. The latest revision is the fixed revision in every Region where the runbook is available, and its revision number varies by Region. To find it, run aws ssm describe-document --name AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 --region <region> --query "Document.LatestVersion". Update any Automation executions, State Manager associations, AWS Config remediation configurations, or other automations pinned to an earlier revision to use the latest revision. 2. Until earlier revisions are removed in your Region, either keep untrusted users from running earlier revisions of the runbook, or keep a trusted Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) in every Region. Earlier revisions inject only when they create this document, so while a trusted one exists, this path is closed in that Region. 3. Review your Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) in any Region where it was first created by an earlier revision of this runbook, not by you. To check, look for any run of this runbook that failed with "DOCUMENT CREATE OR UPDATE FAILED." An injected run always fails with this error. You can also compare the creation date of the document's first version with the start times of runs of this runbook in that Region. Check the document for settings you did not configure, especially shellProfile, Run As (runAsEnabled, runAsDefaultUser), maxSessionDuration, idleSessionTimeout, and the logging destination fields. The fixed runbook updates only the S3 bucket and prefix fields of an existing preferences document, so settings injected earlier remain until you remove them. If you find unexpected settings, restore your trusted preferences and review instances on which Session Manager sessions were started while those settings were active. The AWS Security Bulletin includes commands for this review.

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request.
CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules.

CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

"Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today.

CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml").
Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password.
Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer.

//]]>

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core.

"Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site."

As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances.

According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code.

While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources.

As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, and Drupal allows the installation to proceed after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass.

To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use -

EMFILE, which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open
Database connection exhaustion
TCP source-port exhaustion

"We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said.

"Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL."

This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is made possible because the installer doesn't restrict the file name extension.

"By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file."

While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution.

"Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said.

Hackers Exploited CVSS 10.0 Hex.pm RCE Flaw to Compromise 6 Package Registry ServersSwati KhandelwalNov 25, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from.

The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request.

Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said.

What Hex Users Should Do Now

Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps:

Change your hex.pm password.
Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes.
Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth.
Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system.
Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm.

API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters.

Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it.

Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it.

The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded.

The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established.

A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account.

The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday.

An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world.

The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S.

Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control. Most of these IP addresses are associated with disposable network infrastructure.

The campaign has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. It's suspected that the attackers are relying on agentic harnesses and systems for vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and automatic interaction with compromised assets.

The threat actor has also been observed using tools like Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python scripts to carry out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on victim environments.

"We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created," GreyNoise said.

In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500, a critical flaw in Rejetto HFS, in early October 2026 to obtain control of the server and issue commands, including adding an SSH key to the "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys" file.

Subsequently, GT13 is said to have used the compromised server as a relay for follow-on operations centered around saving command results and exfiltrating data from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attackers also unsuccessfully attempted to deploy a Linux implant named ZULT to the compromised Rejetto HFS server.

"The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server," the cybersecurity company said. "We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets."

Unload security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections
Conduct internal network reconnaissance and attempt lateral movement

WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account.

The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent."

The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below -

Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4)
WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4)
Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3)
Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4)
Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4)
Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2)

These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched.

"Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said.

Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval().

It can also perform the following actions -

Accept queued commands that run shell commands
Read, write, and delete arbitrary files
Query arbitrary database tables
Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes
Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing
Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal.

Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible.

"Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally."

The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors.

Scope: AWS

Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST

Description:

AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document.

We identified CVE-2026-134070, where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions.

Impacted versions: Revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC)

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in a fixed revision of the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3, available in all Regions where the runbook is available. The fixed revision is the latest revision in each Region. Its revision number varies by Region. To find it, run: aws ssm describe-document --name AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 --region <region> --query "Document.LatestVersion" We recommend upgrading to the latest revision and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Update any Automation executions, State Manager associations, AWS Config remediation configurations, or other automations pinned to an earlier revision to use the latest revision.

Any user permitted to run the runbook can choose which revision to run. Earlier revisions remain runnable until AWS deprecates all revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC), beginning January 15, 2027, in every Region and partition. VMware patches 23 flaws, including another critical vCenter authentication bypass

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

Broadcom released advisory VMSA-2026-0011 on November 24, 2026, addressing 23 vulnerabilities across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. The most notable is CVE-2026-123903, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware Directory Service (vmdir) with a CVSS score of 9.8.

Public proof-of-concept code demonstrates that an unauthenticated adversary with network access to a vulnerable vCenter server can create accounts and assign administrator privileges without valid credentials.

No exploitation of CVE-2026-123903 has been reported. However, the vulnerability affects the same vmdir component targeted by CVE-2026-123890, a separate authentication bypass vulnerability exploited as a zero-day by Armory Castle, a suspected China-nexus espionage actor.

Threat summary
On November 24, 2026, Broadcom issued a security advisory VMSA-2026-0011, addressing 23 vulnerabilities across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer.
Four vulnerabilities are rated Critical:

CVE-2026-123903 affecting VMware vCenter
CVE-2026-123910 affecting VMware ESX
CVE-2026-123911 affecting VMware ESX

The same day the advisory was released, a public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-123903 was published. Rapid7 later validated the exploit. At the time of writing, there are no public reports of CVE-2026-123903 being exploited in the wild.
Earlier this month, it was reported that a suspected China-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, exploited CVE-2026-123890 as a zero-day from at least early September 2026 until Broadcom released patches on November 19.
Both vulnerabilities affect VMware Directory Service (vmdir), the identity service that supports vCenter Single Sign-On authentication, but they target different components within the service.

CVE-2026-123890 is reachable through the Distributed Computing Environment / Remote Procedure Call (DCE/RPC) interface used by vCenter Single Sign-On services

CVE-2026-123903 affects the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) service within vmdir

Broadcom describes CVE-2026-123903 as an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows an adversary with network access to a vulnerable vCenter server to gain unauthorized access without valid credentials. Exploitation is remote, requires no authentication or user interaction, and depends only on network access to the affected vCenter deployment.
VMSA-2026-0011 also includes two Critical ESX vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS 9.8 and both affecting the ESX I/O Filter Service:

CVE-2026-123910 (a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability)

CVE-2026-123911 (a use-after-free vulnerability)

An adversary with network access to a vulnerable ESX host can exploit either vulnerability to execute code on the host without first compromising a guest virtual machine.
The advisory also addresses CVE-2026-123912, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the XHCI USB controller affecting ESX, Workstation, and Fusion. Exploitation requires administrator privileges within a virtual machine.
On Workstation and Fusion, where the vulnerability is rated CVSS 9.3, successful exploitation can lead to code execution on the host operating system. On ESX, Broadcom states that impact is contained within the VMX sandbox.
VMSA-2026-0011 also patches CVE-2026-123913, a VMkernel stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability (CVSS 8.2) that requires existing privileges within the VMX process.

title: How to protect against preinstalled Android malware
text:
Threat Response

IntroductionLandscape of preinstalled threatsCorporate environmentUsing Kaspersky solutions to mitigate risks

Introduction
Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage.
We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions.

Landscape of preinstalled threats
The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year.

Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 (download)
Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026.
The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Known modules can steal credentials for messaging and social media apps, intercept calls and text messages, replace links in browsers, siphon off cryptocurrency, and run a reverse proxy on the infected device. It’s worth stressing that by loading additional modules, attackers get virtually unlimited capabilities.
Keenadu is another preinstalled backdoor we discovered, which appeared relatively recently. The earliest known firmware version that contains this malware dates back to 2023. Even so, the number of devices infected with Keenadu is considerable: according to our data, more than 220,000 devices were infected in the first ten months of 2026.
Keenadu is similar to Triada in many ways, especially in its main architectural feature: once it’s on a device, attackers can download additional modules with any functionality and inject them into target apps. SWITZERLAND CONFIRMS FIRST AI-AGENT CYBERATTACKS ON LOCAL ORGANISATIONS
Pierluigi Paganini

November 25, 2026
Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours.

Switzerland ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has now seen these attacks firsthand. In recent days, it received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents. The victims include critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent.” reads the report published by NCSC. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

What stands out is the result. In every AI-assisted attack known to the NCSC, the attackers successfully compromised the victims’ IT systems. The agency sees these incidents as more than isolated cases, warning that they mark a shift in the cyber threat landscape.

The attackers used what the NCSC calls “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”. These AI agents can search for vulnerabilities, choose attack tools, assess the results and decide what to do next, all with limited human input. Security teams also use the same software for penetration testing, which makes these tools dual-use.

The targets aren’t exotic. The agents go after standard or easily guessed passwords, known flaws in software, and systems connected to the internet.

Broadcom has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-123903, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting VMware vCenter Server. The flaw resides in VMware Directory Service, or vmdir, and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical.

A remote attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter deployment can exploit the weakness to bypass authentication and obtain unauthorized access without valid credentials or user interaction. Because vCenter acts as the centralized management layer for VMware virtual infrastructure, compromise of its identity and directory services can expose highly privileged administrative functionality.

The vulnerability was disclosed on November 24, 2026 as part of VMSA-2026-0011, a broad security release addressing 23 flaws across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, Tools, Cloud Foundation, and Avi Load Balancer. CVE-2026-123903 is particularly notable because it follows CVE-2026-123890, another CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the same VMware Directory Service that was disclosed only days earlier and had already been exploited as a zero-day by the China-nexus ARMORY CASTLE group. Broadcom states that the two vulnerabilities are separate issues and should not be treated as the same attack path.

CVE-2026-123903 affects VMware vCenter deployments across multiple currently supported and legacy product branches, including vCenter 8.0, vCenter components included with VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 9.x, Cloud Foundation 5.x, and affected Telco Cloud products. title: Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR): Turning Sigma Alerts into ATT&CK-Mapped Attack Chains
text:
En

SOC Prime Platform

November 25, 2026
6 min read

Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR) are correlation rules that sit one level above standard Sigma detections. Instead of matching a single log event, a Higher Order Sigma rule links the Sigma rules that fire on one host into an attack chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

Most SOC teams already run hundreds of Sigma rules. Each flags one suspicious step, such as an encoded PowerShell command or a new service install, but analysts still have to work out which alerts belong to the same intrusion. HOSR moves that reasoning into the detection content itself, so multi-stage attack detection starts before anyone opens the alert queue.

Contact Sales

What Is Higher Order Sigma?

Higher Order Sigma is a correlation layer for Sigma: rules whose inputs are the matches of other Sigma rules rather than raw events. SOC Prime introduced Higher Order Sigma rules in July 2026 and began a gradual rollout across its products.

Each Higher Order Sigma rule is built around an Active Threat, SOC Prime’s curated intelligence item on a current campaign or malware family. The rule takes the detection rules attached to that threat and orders them using the threat’s Attack Flow, a sequence of adversary techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The result describes how the whole attack unfolds, not just what one step looks like.

The name echoes higher-order functions in programming, which take other functions as input. A standard Sigma rule asks whether a suspicious event happened. A Higher Order Sigma rule asks whether the steps of a known attack are happening together, on the same machine or same user, within a short time.

In SOC Prime’s design, attack chains are authored by human experts as higher-order rules that correlate on ATT&CK techniques and on sequences of lower-level Sigma rules. Every rule is plain YAML, so detection engineers can read and review it like any other Sigma rule.

How Does Standard Sigma Differ from Higher Order Sigma?

A standard Sigma rule checks one event against field conditions. A Higher Order Sigma rule checks a sequence of Sigma matches against an attack’s expected progression.

Standard Sigma is the vendor-agnostic YAML format detection engineers use to describe suspicious log events once and translate them to any SIEM, EDR, or data lake. Its strength is precision on a single log source. Its limit is that each rule sees one event in isolation, so ten related detections arrive as ten unrelated alerts.

The Sigma specification does offer correlation rules, such as event_count, value_count, temporal, and temporal_ordered, which group matches by a field within a timespan. They are useful, but each one is written by hand for a specific use case, and temporal types expect every referenced rule to match:

title: Admin share access followed by remote service install

correlation:

type: temporal_ordered

rules:

– smb_admin_share_access

– remote_service_creation

group-by:

– ComputerName

timespan: 10m

If the attacker skips one step, a rule like this stays silent. Higher Order Sigma builds on the same correlation idea but is derived from threat intelligence, organized by ATT&CK stage, and designed to tolerate gaps.

The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense

4 min read

The New Reality of AI AttackersAI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. We have observed attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making. In one campaign that we observed, a highly persistent threat actor utilizing AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days whereas normal attackers usually do dozens of commands with a few scripts for similar time periods.The behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents is staggering. In one attack we observed, humans acted followed by an agentic AI attacker. In the first (human attacker) phase, time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds. The hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and demonstrated environment confusion. On the other hand, in the agentic phase of the attack, we observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds.When an AI agent is instructed to execute aspects of an attack, it rapidly scans networks, attempts to escalate privileges and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in. Because of AI’s machine-speed execution, our Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) metrics must improve considerably. Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If we wait hours to react, an AI agent can have already enumerated our cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted our data.To effectively defend against AI-powered attacks, defenders must employ AI-powered tools. This should be done right where the attacks happen. Defenders should also strive to understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations, whether fully autonomous or partially controlled by a human.The Power of Edge AI and Layered DetectionTo counter adversaries operating at automated speeds, defense must occur where the attack takes place. Leveraging AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW), is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally.Edge AI is also exceptionally fast. In our own product deployment, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than taking minutes like agentic LLMs. It can function independently of cloud access or continuous network connectivity. This capabilities shift is crucial for several key reasons:
Even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently, local edge AI maintains detection coverage
It enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage
It safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis
The Defender’s Ultimate Advantage: Knowledge and ContextDespite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness that affects any attacker: They enter your environment without information. To operate, they must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration. This is where defenders hold the ultimate upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.Winning against machine-speed adversaries requires turning the advantage into real-time detection through automated data fusion and detection. By collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalization can map these distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema. title: How a Fake Job Interview Led to the $6.34 Billion Binance Theft
text: Jump to sectionIn September 2026, a software engineer at Binance got a message on a job-hunting site. Someone posing as a Project Director wanted to talk about a role. What followed looked like a normal hiring process. First came a live video interview with an HR representative, then a second round with someone claiming to be the CEO. Near the end of that call, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment. He did it on his work computer, and malicious code gave the attackers access to his machine and credentials.The attackers moved laterally through the Binance organization, and on October 29 they stole about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency. Binance's report lists the fake interview as one step in a longer chain. The developer wasn't the end goal. A candidate who runs an assignment on a work laptop hands the attackers a machine inside their employer's network.The FBI attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, the same North Korean group it blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025. Blockchain analysts at TRM Labs and Chainalysis also linked the two thefts, saying the attack matched Bybit in a few ways:The attackers started preparing at least 36 hours ahead.The signatures were produced in advance as a batch, then used in one burst.Three small Tornado Cash withdrawals funded the attackers' operator wallet.None of these alone proves it's the same group. They're patterns TRM has seen in earlier North Korean heists, and TRM paired them with on-chain and off-chain intelligence it didn't detail. Chainalysis said its strongest evidence was watching Binance funds mix in real time with proceeds from the roughly $357 million theft from crypto exchange Bitget in late September. Elliptic had already tied that hack to TraderTraitor in a preliminary assessment, citing on-chain overlaps with the Bybit attack. That chain of overlaps, from Binance to Bitget to Bybit, is the clearest public link between the attacks.The fake interview that compromised Binance follows the same playbook as Contagious Interview, a North Korean campaign that's been luring developers with fake job offers since at least 2023. That matters for defenders, but not as much as you might hope. Being able to detect Contagious Interview (or PolinRider, more on that below) activity is a good start. But it won't reliably catch TraderTraitor, which tailors its attacks to a small number of high-value targets. And no tool on the market today will stop a developer from consuming a malicious repository in the first place.TraderTraitor vs. Contagious Interview vs. PolinRiderThese names are easy to mix up, and they can overlap in practice. Contagious Interview is one of the main ways PolinRider gets onto a developer's machine, and TraderTraitor runs the same fake-interview playbook against higher-value targets. NameCategoryWhat it isTraderTraitorGroupAlso known as Slow Pisces, Jade Sleet and UNC4899, this group targets developers at large crypto organizations. It runs its own version of the Contagious Interview playbook, with coding challenges that are mostly Python or JavaScript and payloads that go only to vetted targets.Contagious InterviewCampaign (tactic)A playbook that's been run against everyone from freelancers to CTOs since at least 2023: a fake recruiter, a fake interview and a coding test that installs malware. Its operators are tracked as Famous Chollima, WaterPlum and UNC5342.PolinRiderCampaign (tactic)A self-propagating persistence campaign. Once one developer is infected, it spreads North Korean malware to others who never dealt with a North Korean operative directly. Infections can come from Contagious Interview, a poisoned OSS package, or a compromised GitHub collaborator.How the Binance attack unfoldedBinance's report lays the attack out as a series of steps, but it reads more clearly as three phases. We think each phase was likely run by a different North Korean team, with each one handing off to the next.Outside of this attack, Binance also […]

These issues warned maintainers that wallet keys tied to their projects had appeared in a leaked dataset. The warning was a trap. It pushed readers to move funds into attacker-controlled wallets and to submit their seed phrases, private keys or keystore files to a fake "WalletGuard" verification page that sent everything it received to the attacker. We stopped the collector, identified at least two victims, and warned the targeted projects.The campaign disproportionately targeted cryptocurrency wallets, blockchain clients, smart-contract frameworks, exchanges, security tools and Web3 developer libraries. Fix: No customer action required, 1Password says. Treat unexpected 1Password invite or recovery emails as phishing and open the app yourself (1Password incident update).
Exploited yet? Yes, the data was taken, per 1Password, Nov 25. Use of the stolen invite and recovery tokens: Unknown outside 1Password. 1Password says it found “no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens,” Nov 25.

Do this first: If you get an email, text or call about a 1Password invitation or account recovery that you didn’t start, treat it as phishing. Don’t click the link. Open the 1Password app, or type 1password.com yourself, and check from there.

What happened

1Password says it began investigating on Nov 19, 2026, after signs that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. It disclosed the incident in a blog post dated Nov 25, six days later, and on X at 11:28 AM CT.
The attacker used that account to reach source code and “push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” per the blog post.
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and got into 1Password’s CI/CD system, the automated system that builds its software. 1Password says CI/CD holds “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has rotated every credential that may have been exposed.
1Password says it disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, lengthened the codes in invite and recovery emails, tightened GitHub, CI/CD and device controls, and brought in outside security experts. It hasn’t named those experts or published their findings.

What 1Password says was taken
All of this comes from 1Password’s blog post, Nov 25:

Names and the email addresses customers use to sign in.
Account and user IDs, plus when each account was created and last signed in.
Public keys. 1Password says these are public by design.
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, part of how 1Password checks your sign-in. 1Password says they “cannot be used to access your account.”
“Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.”
Other internal account data that 1Password calls non-secret, such as version and file ID numbers.

What 1Password says was not taken
These are 1Password’s claims. No independent report has confirmed them yet.

title: 1Password says a hacker used an employee’s GitHub account to take customer data
text:
Dave Barr reports:
Malicious code sent through one employee’s corporate GitHub account made 1Password’s own backend services download customer records, the company said in an incident post on Wednesday, November 25. The intruder also copied source code from private repositories and got into the CI/CD system, the pipeline that builds and ships software. 1Password started investigating on November 19.
So 1Password was hacked. The line it draws runs between its backend and your vault. Vault contents, the keys protecting them, account recovery keys, the apps and the browser extensions weren’t affected, it says, and it doesn’t store your account password or Secret Key in the first place.
The downloaded records cover a subset of users. Names and email addresses are in them, along with account and user IDs, account creation dates and last sign-in times. Public keys, other non-secret metadata and the settings used by Secure Remote Password, a login protocol, were copied too. According to 1Password, the keys are public by design and those settings can’t be used to get into your account.

1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe

Zack Whittaker

10:49 AM PST · November 25, 2026

Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

Nearly 2 billion credentials exposed in a publicly accessible database
ResearchWritten byJeremiah FowlerNovember 24, 20269 min read Cybersecurity Researcher Jeremiah Fowler uncovered a data leak involving two billion credentials from what appears to be an illicit underground marketplace or possibly a legitimate research dataset and shared his findings with ExpressVPN. We are publishing his report to help the public stay informed and protected as part of our ongoing effort to make the web a safer place.
What the exposed database contained
I recently discovered a publicly exposed database that was neither password-protected nor encrypted. It contained approximately 2 billion credentials, including email addresses, login names, passwords, and more. In a limited sample of the records I reviewed, I observed logs that may contain saved application credentials, browser passwords, cookies, session tokens, authentication artifacts, device information, and other application identifiers.
In volume and scope, this is the largest collection of credentials I have discovered in my years as a security researcher, and it reinforces the growing threat that malware poses globally. This 2 billion record dataset is more than 13 times the size of a previous exposure of 149 million logins and passwords I reported earlier this year. That dataset was mostly limited to usernames, passwords, and login URLs. This one goes further, with session tokens, cookies, and device data that give attackers more ways in than a password alone.
The database contained 8,471 folders with credentials and account information in plaintext. Some documents were segmented by country and included abbreviations in the file names, such as US, UK, FR, DE, ES, and MX. An estimated 400,000 documents appeared to come from more advanced malware that created separate folders for individual victims. These included folders named applications, cookies, edge, important files, and operating systems, as well as .txt documents labeled system, process, clipboard, brute force, passwords, and more. Together, these could provide a detailed profile of each victim and their devices and accounts, revealing a much wider range of potential attack paths beyond those available through username, login URL, and password data alone.
I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.
The database contained no information identifying who owned or managed the exposed records. The files referenced or indicated multiple suspected cybercriminal data sources or underground credential operations as the original sources. I immediately reported my discovery to the hosting provider, and public access was restricted several days later. While I did not download the exposed files, they remained publicly accessible long enough for me to query common domains and extensions, estimate account totals, and put the discovery into perspective by domain or service.
Estimated records by service and domain

text:
The attacker also obtained keys that allowed Todoist to connect to other services and had access to some items from connected Outlook mailboxes. Todoist says it blocked his access and began notifying affected users on November 24th.
How the breach occurred
According to Todoist's report, the initial breach was caused by stolen credentials for a system used to make changes to the app's code. The attacker changed automated processes in three places where the code is stored. This gave him more credentials and used an employee's work account to access the company's online systems.
It was able to read the code, but researchers did not detect any changes to the app's code. Security monitoring detected an unexpected administrator account on November 23, hours after the user data was downloaded.
Which elements were affected?
The old saved password formats were not readable as plain text. However, the old storage method made it easier to guess passwords. Todoist has stopped using it and has found no evidence that the attacker logged into accounts in this user group.

↳ READ ALSO HACKS.GR / RELATED

Cyber ​​Attacks & Data Breaches An unknown attacker copied account details of some 1Password customers
↗

Approximately 0,003% of users were affected by the acquisition of Todoist and Slack login keys. Approximately 0,001% of accounts were targeted for access credentials within tasks, comments, and attachment names. Todoist found no evidence of a mass download of user tasks and comments.
About another 0,001% of users were affected via the Todoist tool for Outlook. The attacker requested sender information, message subjects, up to 255 characters of their body text, and information about attachments.
What users should do
Todoist says that those who didn't receive a notification don't need to do anything. If the company disabled your password, reset it from the official Todoist page and change it in other services where you used it. Google and Apple passwords were not affected.
If Todoist has revoked a connection key that one of your automated programs uses, replace it with a new one from Settings → Connections → Developer. If you had keys or other access details saved in Todoist, revoke them and request new ones from the service that issued them. Deleting a task or comment does not revoke items that may have already been copied.
Todoist notifications are sent from the address no-reply@notify.todoist.comAccording to the company, they do not ask for a password or program installation. If a message seems suspicious to you, contact Todoist directly instead of responding to it.

title: ITDR : pourquoi protéger les identités de votre entreprise ?
text:
L’ITDR, pour Identity Threat Detection and Response, permet de détecter les menaces visant les identités numériques et d’organiser la réponse aux compromissions. Pour votre entreprise, l’enjeu est concret : un attaquant disposant d’un compte valide peut accéder à des ressources avec les autorisations de son titulaire. La protection des postes de travail doit donc s’accompagner d’une surveillance des identités et de leur utilisation.
Un compte légitime peut servir une attaque
Les identités numériques donnent accès aux messageries, aux applications métiers et aux documents partagés. Lorsqu’un attaquant récupère des identifiants par un hameçonnage (phishing), par un credential stuffing (fuite de données), par des actions de social hacking, ou compromet un compte existant par une attaque par force brute, il peut emprunter ces accès pour voler, supprimer ou compromettre des données sensibles. Certaines opérations malveillantes utilisent alors les fonctions ordinaires des outils de l’entreprise, sans nécessiter l’installation immédiate d’un logiciel malveillant.
Ce type d’attaque est très difficile à repérer, car elle échappe aux antivirus traditionnels : l’ITDR aide à repérer les usages suspects et à intervenir avant que la compromission ne s’étende.
Des conséquences liées aux droits du compte
Prenons un scénario fictif : un attaquant récupère les identifiants d’un collaborateur puis consulte les dossiers auxquels celui-ci a accès. Si les autorisations sont trop larges, il peut atteindre des informations sans rapport avec les missions du salarié.
Avec un compte administrateur compromis, le risque s’étend à la modification des accès ou à la création de nouveaux comptes. L’attaquant peut aussi chercher à progresser vers d’autres systèmes : ce sont les mouvements latéraux. Les conséquences dépendent donc des ressources accessibles et des privilèges associés à chaque identité.
Comment l’ITDR contribue-t-il à détecter une compromission ?
Une solution ITDR analyse les activités liées aux identités pour identifier des signes d’utilisation malveillante. Une connexion inhabituelle, une modification de privilèges ou une création de compte peuvent déclencher une investigation.
Replacer les anomalies dans leur contexte
Un horaire inhabituel ne prouve pas une attaque : un collaborateur peut travailler tard. En revanche, une connexion nocturne depuis un pays inhabituel, associée à la consultation de documents sans lien avec ses missions, mérite une investigation. La qualification consiste à croiser ces indices avec les habitudes du compte et les événements observés sur les équipements pour évaluer la probabilité d’une compromission.
Cette contextualisation aide les équipes à distinguer une activité autorisée d’une compromission probable. La qualité des informations collectées et la couverture des systèmes d’identité conditionnent cette capacité d’analyse.
Préparer les actions de réponse
Selon les capacités de la solution et les systèmes concernés, la réponse peut comprendre :

la suspension d’un compte,
la révocation de sessions,
le changement de ses moyens d’authentification.

Vous devriez définir à l’avance qui peut autoriser ces actions : bloquer un compte utilisé par une application métier peut ainsi interrompre un service stratégique pour votre entreprise, vos partenaires ou vos clients. La procédure doit tenir compte de cette dépendance.
Organiser une protection adaptée à votre entreprise
Vous pouvez commencer par examiner les comptes administrateurs, les accès des prestataires et les comptes devenus inutiles. Pour chacun, l’équipe informatique devrait pouvoir identifier un responsable, justifier les droits accordés et expliquer comment l’activité est surveillée.
L’authentification multifacteur réduit le risque d’accès frauduleux, particulièrement avec des méthodes résistantes au phishing. Elle s’inscrit dans une protection qui associe plusieurs fonctions.

Rôles principaux des dispositifs de sécurité des identités et des […]

The Vault Is Still Fine

Back in June I wrote The Vault Is Fine, which was mostly me dunking on LastPass for being LastPass. Their vendor Klue got popped, customer contact details and support case data walked out the door, and the official line was that the vaults weren't touched. Which, sure. The vault is fine, until it isn't.

In that post I pointed people toward the alternatives. 1Password was near the top of that list.

So naturally, on November 25: 1Password says hackers broke into its internal systems.

Yeah. I saw it too.

The Scorecard (Again)
Here's what 1Password says happened, from their own disclosure:

November 19: They start investigating signs that someone had taken over an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The how: The attacker used that access to push malicious code to backend servers, and that code pulled customer data.

November 25: Public disclosure. The blog post goes up, and the press picks it up the same day.

And what got taken, per Newsweek's breakdown of the disclosure:

Names and the email addresses customers use to sign in
Internal account and user IDs, account creation dates, last sign-in dates
Security tokens sitting in some invitation, setup, and account recovery emails
Public keys and sign-in protocol parameters, which 1Password says are harmless on their own

What wasn't taken: vaults, account passwords, Secret Keys. 1Password's line is that vault contents were never accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

If you read the June post, you can already hum along. A way in that wasn't the product itself. Customer metadata gone. Vaults fine. It's the same song with a different band.

And the way in should sound familiar too. LastPass 2022 started with a compromised developer laptop. This one started with a compromised developer GitHub account. The front door is fine. It's always the guy with keys to the back office.

Where It's Actually Different
I'm not going to pretend this is LastPass 2.0, because it isn't, and the reason it isn't is the whole point of the June post.

The architecture held. 1Password's vaults are locked with your account password plus a 34-character Secret Key that's generated on your device and that 1Password never has a copy of. So even in the worst case, where an attacker walks off with encrypted vault data, they're not brute-forcing your password alone. They'd need a secret that isn't on 1Password's servers. Compare that to LastPass, where the only thing standing between an attacker and roughly 30 million stolen vaults was one password and an iteration count that had been flagged as dangerously low for years.

That's what "architecture matters" actually looks like when it's tested. Not a marketing slide. An incident where the bad guys got real access and the vaults still weren't on the table.

They also did the cleanup work you'd hope for: killed the compromised account and token, rotated internal credentials including in their build and release pipeline, brought in outside security people, and stretched the account recovery code from a six-digit number to a 10-character alphanumeric code. That last one tells you they took the recovery-token exposure seriously, and good.

Props Where Due
Credit where it's earned: six days from "something's off" to a public write-up that names what was taken is miles ahead of LastPass. LastPass told everyone there was "no evidence" of vault access in 2022 and then, four months later, admitted encrypted vault backups for roughly 30 million users were gone. That's not a disclosure. That's a slow leak.

It's also more in line with how Dashlane handled its brute-force incident at the end of May: say what happened, say what's affected, update it, close it out. That's the bar. 1Password cleared it.

But Six Days Is an Eternity
Here's the thing though. Six days is fast for a corporate disclosure. Six days to a scammer is an eternity.

Think about what that list actually is. It's not random emails scraped off a forum. It's a verified roster […]

Ancien reporter, député de Paris et fondateur du parti Révolution écologique pour le vivant (REV)

Les crimes commis par les autorités israéliennes envers la population de Gaza, régulièrement qualifiés de génocide par plusieurs ONG, imposent progressivement une frontière morale entre ceux qui les cautionnent et ceux qui les dénoncent. De nombreux États ou personnalités publiques restent silencieux face à ces évènements, alors même que les violences de masse perpétrées envers les populations les plus vulnérables (enfants, femmes et personnes âgées) sont un fait documenté qui constitue une atteinte fondamentale aux droits humains.

Cette absence de considération pour les victimes est amplifiée par la silenciation des voix palestiniennes, tant dans les médias privés que publics. Cette crise morale est symptomatique de la dérive d’un monde occidental qui s’écarte des principes qu’il prétend porter : alors même qu’il revendique la défense des droits humains et des libertés individuelles, l’Occident est frappé par l’affaiblissement de la démocratie, la montée de l’extrême droite et plus largement la multiplication des atteintes au vivant.

Comment expliquer que le conflit israélo-palestinien ait un tel impact sur les rapports sociaux ? L’impunité israélienne à Gaza est-elle le symptôme d’un effondrement moral de l’Occident ? Comment qualifier l’omerta qui règne autour de la question palestinienne dans les médias ? Quel lien peut-on établir entre le combat pour les droits humains et l’antispécisme ?

Autant d’enjeux abordés avec Aymeric Caron, ancien reporter, député de Paris et fondateur du parti Révolution écologique pour le vivant (REV).

title: RETEX et sécurité économique, la France sait-elle apprendre de ses ingérences ?
text:
RETEX et sécurité économique, la France sait-elle apprendre de ses ingérences ?

François Wald

Publié le
25/11/2026

Analyse

7 min

Source : Ministère chargé de l’Économie – Célia Bonnin

Le Service de l’information stratégique et de la sécurité économiques (SISSE) enregistre plus de 800 alertes de sécurité économique en 2026. Aucun dispositif ne transforme pourtant ces incidents, de façon systématique, en savoir partagé. L’Allemagne, la Suisse, les Pays-Bas et le Royaume-Uni ouvrent des pistes, sans avoir résolu cette question.

Le 24 septembre 2026, Bercy a tenu les premières Assises de la sécurité économique. Le SISSE y a présenté sa doctrine de sécurité économique et annoncé plus de 800 alertes en 2026, contre 750 en 2024-2025. Déposé en juillet, le rapport Rodwell-Thiériot-Plassard recommandait d’abord de sensibiliser toujours davantage. La capacité à tirer les leçons des attaques subies, ce que les armées appellent le retour d’expérience (RETEX), reste en revanche peu traitée.

Le RETEX, chaînon manquant du dispositif français

Selon la doctrine interarmées PIA-7.7, le RETEX part d’un constat de terrain, dont l’analyse permet de dégager des leçons. Seule leurs traduction en plan d’action, suivie d’une vérification de son effet, produit une « leçon apprise ». La veille signale une menace, tandis que le RETEX explique comment une attaque a réussi et ce qu’il faut changer.

Le monde économique dispose de quelques briques. Depuis plus de dix ans, la Direction générale de la sécurité intérieure (DGSI) diffuse des « flashs ingérence économique » tirés de cas réels anonymisés, par exemple sur l’intelligence artificielle ou les applications étrangères. Ces supports restent toutefois descendants. Ils diffusent des leçons identifiées, sans garantir qu’elles deviennent des leçons apprises.

Deux freins expliquent ce retard. Selon une étude commandée par le renseignement suisse, les entreprises renoncent à signaler les cas d’espionnage par crainte pour leur réputation et pour leurs résultats. L’instabilité institutionnelle aggrave la difficulté. La Délégation interministérielle à l’intelligence économique (D2IE), créée en 2009, n’a pas survécu à la réorganisation de 2016, l’une des nombreuses restructurations intervenues depuis le rapport Martre de 1994. Certaines entreprises ont bâti leur propre culture du RETEX, mais celle-ci ne dépasse pas leurs murs.

Allemagne et Suisse, deux modèles de partenariat

Face aux mêmes difficultés, l’Allemagne a choisi d’institutionnaliser le dialogue entre l’État et les entreprises. Le 18 mars 2026, Berlin a adopté sa première Nationale Wirtschaftsschutzstrategie (stratégie nationale de protection de l’économie), qui organise le soutien de l’État aux entreprises face aux menaces physiques, numériques et hybrides, au premier rang desquelles l’espionnage et le sabotage économiques. Elle prévoit un tableau de situation partagé et un échange d’informations dans les deux sens. Elle s’appuie sur le VSW (Verband für Sicherheit in der Wirtschaft), fédération des associations de sécurité des entreprises qui se présente comme l’interface entre les entreprises, les services de sécurité et le monde politique. La stratégie de Berlin prévoit aussi des échanges de bonnes pratiques et une plateforme de mise en commun des menaces, mais aucun dispositif de signalement des incidents ouvert à toutes les entreprises : le modèle allemand s’arrête ainsi au seuil du RETEX.

La Suisse a pris le problème par l’autre bout, en s’attaquant d’abord à la crainte du signalement. Dès 2004, le programme Prophylax a permis au Service de renseignement de la Confédération (SRC) de conseiller entreprises et instituts de recherche. Le SRC s’engage à traiter chaque cas d’espionnage de manière confidentielle, ce qui rassure les victimes. En 2020, une étude de l’Université de Berne commandée par le SRC a mesuré l’ampleur de la menace : 15 % des entreprises interrogées en ligne, et environ un tiers de celles rencontrées en entretien, […]

Alexander Stonor

Chercheur associé à l’IRIS

Cartographie par Thomas Cattin
Doctorant en géopolitique et cartographe, Cassini

Les matières premières minérales occupent une place croissante dans les politiques énergétiques, industrielles et de sécurité des États. L’électrification des usages et la fabrication des équipements nécessaires à la décarbonation accroissent les besoins en métaux, auxquels s’ajoutent ceux du numérique et de la défense. L’extraction et la transformation de ces matières restent concentrées dans un nombre limité de pays. L’Afrique subsaharienne détient près de 30 % des réserves mondiales prouvées de minerais critiques, or sa contribution aux échanges n’est pas proportionnelle. En 2023, le continent représentait 10,6 % de la valeur des exportations mondiales de minerais bruts et semi-transformés. La composition de ces exportations traduit également son positionnement dans les premières étapes des chaînes de valeur, puisque 96 % des minerais critiques exportés étaient commercialisés sous une forme brute (24 %) ou semi-transformée (72 %).

Ce rapport vise à comprendre comment les flux de ressources minérales africaines sont structurés par la compétition des grandes puissances, l’affirmation des gouvernements nationaux et les risques inhérents à leur exploitation et à leur transport. La première partie examine les stratégies chinoises, étatsuniennes et européennes pour déterminer comment leurs investissements, leurs contrats commerciaux et leur présence dans les infrastructures influencent l’organisation des approvisionnements, depuis l’extraction jusqu’à la transformation et à la commercialisation des minerais. La deuxième partie étudie les moyens dont disposent les États producteurs pour orienter les investissements, développer la transformation locale et peser sur les conditions de commercialisation de leurs ressources. Les études de cas portent sur les principaux producteurs africains de minerais nécessaires aux technologies bas carbone identifiés par l’AIE et pour lesquels le continent représente plus de 10 % de la production mondiale. Cette sélection comprend la République démocratique du Congo (RDC) pour le cuivre et le cobalt, la Guinée pour la bauxite, le Zimbabwe pour le lithium et l’Afrique du Sud pour le manganèse et les platinoïdes. L’étude de la Namibie complète cet ensemble en intégrant l’uranium, afin de prendre en compte les besoins d’approvisionnement du nucléaire et sa contribution à la production d’électricité bas carbone. La troisième partie examine comment les contraintes logistiques, énergétiques, climatiques et sociopolitiques peuvent interrompre la production, retarder les projets ou empêcher l’acheminement des minerais. Elle distingue les difficultés qui affectent les approvisionnements existants de celles qui compromettent le développement de nouvelles capacités, afin d’apprécier la contribution effective des ressources africaines à la sécurité des approvisionnements.

Raphaël Derréal

Publié le
25/11/2026

« To make war, you need intelligence. But to win you need talent and material »

For whom the Bell Tolls, E. Hemingway, 1940

Mardi 23 janvier avait lieu la première édition des Rencontres de l’armement.  Organisée par le Conseil général de l’armement, elle a réuni des représentants du secteur public et privé. Un événement amené à être réitéré.

C’est à l’Ecole militaire de Paris devant un amphithéâtre complet qu’ont été abordés les enjeux stratégiques de l’armement à l’horizon 2027-2032.

Ils comprennent notamment la mutation nécessaire de certains programmes militaires longs et complexes qui nécessitent aujourd’hui un besoin d’adaptation constant. Ce besoin se fait surtout sentir dans les domaines des technologies de pointe et de l’information, afin d’éviter une obsolescence dès la livraison.

Le passage à la production de guerre de matériel militaire ainsi que la répartition des investissements sont aussi le centre des discussions. Les institutions militaires cherchent en effet à créer une capacité de production de matériel tandis que les privés cherchent à sécuriser leurs investissements.

In fine, de nombreux entrepreneurs du privé soulignent l’impossibilité actuelle de développer des technologies de défense en se basant uniquement sur le marché français voire européen. La faible demande et la compétitivité obligent les entreprises à s’exporter à l’international. Cela crée donc des potentiels transferts de technologies non souhaités, et soulève de nombreuses questions de dépendance dans les chaînes de valeur.
